USGS ComCat · M4.5+ · 1976–2026 plotting…

Four Hundred Thousand Earthquakes

There is no map underneath this. Every mark is one earthquake, placed where it happened. The continents never appear — but the plates do.

The catalogue

Fifty years of listening to the ground

I downloaded every earthquake of magnitude 4.5 or greater that the United States Geological Survey has recorded since 1 January 1976, plus four dense regional catalogues reaching down to magnitude 1. Then I asked the pile of numbers what it knew.

What follows is not a summary of seismology. It is what falls out of one archive when you take it seriously — including the places where the archive is lying to you, which turn out to be some of the most interesting places in it.

457,408events analysed
283,681global records, M4.5+
50.7years of coverage
700.9km, deepest hypocentre
9.1largest magnitude, twice

The global file is not purely tectonic. Sifting it by event type turns up 470 nuclear explosions, 71 volcanic eruptions, eleven chemical blasts, four mine collapses, three rock bursts and three landslides — all of them large enough to shake the planet measurably. We will come back to the bombs. First, the law that governs everything else.

Frequency & magnitude

One straight line, four decades wide

Count the earthquakes at each magnitude and something implausibly tidy happens. Plot the logarithm of the count against magnitude and the points fall on a straight line — not approximately, but for four full orders of magnitude, from eighty-five thousand events at M5.0 down to the two M9.1s that bracket the whole period.

This is the Gutenberg–Richter relation, and its slope has a name: the b-value. Fitting the catalogue by maximum likelihood gives

b = 1.078 ± 0.004

which is to say: for every step of one magnitude unit, earthquakes become about twelve times rarer. There is no characteristic size of earthquake. There is no scale at which the pattern changes. The same rule that governs a tremor you would not feel governs the one that moved Japan eight feet east.

The straight line is also a forecast. Extrapolate it and you get the rate of earthquakes the Earth should produce at sizes too rare to have been observed often. Compare that prediction against what actually happened over the last half-century and the agreement is uncomfortable in its accuracy: the law predicts 7,088 events at M6.0 or above, and the catalogue holds 7,129.

Where the line breaks. Below about M4.7 the observed counts fall below the fitted line. Small earthquakes have not stopped happening; the network has stopped hearing all of them. Every catalogue has a magnitude of completeness, and reading a catalogue below its own completeness is the most common way to be wrong about earthquakes. It will happen twice more in this piece, both times on purpose.
Location

The plates draw themselves

Plot every epicentre and you do not get a scatter. You get a map — of something that is not the map you expected. A faint outline of the continents is laid underneath so you can find your way around, but take it away and almost nothing is lost: the earthquakes owe the coastlines nothing. What appears instead is a network of thin bright seams — the boundaries between the tectonic plates, traced out by a half-century of failures along them.

Colour the points by how deep they were and the picture gains a third dimension. Deep earthquakes are not scattered among the shallow ones; they sit in narrow bands behind the trenches, on the far side from the ocean, marking the path of a slab of seafloor descending into the mantle. Switch the shallow events off and what remains is a set of disconnected arcs — the Andes, the Kurils, Tonga, the Marianas, the Hindu Kush — every one of them a subduction zone seen edge-on.

The three bands are not arbitrary slices. They are different physics. Above about 70 km, rock is cold and brittle and fails by ordinary friction. Between 70 and 300 km the pressure is far too high for friction to work at all, and earthquakes happen anyway — most likely because water driven out of hydrated minerals in the sinking slab briefly lets the rock slip. Below 300 km even that mechanism fails, and yet the earthquakes continue, all the way to 700 kilometres, where they stop abruptly and completely.

Depth

Where the earthquakes stop

Seventy-seven per cent of recorded earthquakes happen in the top 70 kilometres of the planet — a skin about one per cent of the way to the centre. Another eighteen per cent occur between 70 and 300 km. The remaining five per cent go deeper, and then, at approximately 700 kilometres, the Earth goes silent. The deepest event in fifty years of records sits at 700.9 km, beneath Fiji.

Below that line the mantle is still solid rock under enormous stress. It simply stops producing earthquakes, because the mineral transformation that allows deep rupture has run to completion and there is nothing left to transform.

The b-value changes with depth too, and it changes in a way that says something about stress. Shallow crustal earthquakes give b = 1.04. Deep-focus earthquakes below 300 km give b = 0.88 — a flatter slope, meaning proportionally more large events. Low b-values are associated with high differential stress, which is exactly what you would expect of rock being forced through the mantle transition zone.

Geography of the law

The slope is not the same everywhere

The Gutenberg–Richter law holds globally with b = 1.078. But b is an average over a planet, and the planet is not uniform. Fit it separately in every 2° × 2° neighbourhood that contains enough earthquakes to support a fit, and the value ranges from 0.65 to 1.78.

That range matters. Because b is the slope, a region with b = 0.8 produces roughly three times as many M7s per M5 as a region with b = 1.3. Two places can have identical rates of small earthquakes and quite different rates of destructive ones.

The pattern is not random, and the cleanest way to show that is to stop drawing boxes on a map and use somebody else's classification instead. Peter Bird's 2003 plate model divides the planet's 260,795 kilometres of plate boundary into seven kinds. Assigning every earthquake to its nearest boundary step and re-fitting b within each kind gives a result that no amount of eyeballing would produce as convincingly.

Ridges and transforms sit next to each other, alternating along every mid-ocean spreading system, and they behave differently. Ridge segments are hot, thin and weak: they break often and small. The transforms that offset them are cooler and can store more strain before failing, so a larger share of their earthquakes are big ones. The b-value is reading the temperature and strength of the rock, which is why it varies at all.

What this analysis cannot do. Assignment is by nearest boundary step, which is a crude instrument. The 2004 Sumatra M9.1 lands 75 km from a step Bird classifies as continental rift, so it is filed under rifts rather than subduction — and because that one earthquake carries 13.8 per cent of fifty years of global moment, filing it in the wrong drawer moves a fifth of the moment budget. Event rates and b-values average over tens of thousands of events and are robust to this. Moment shares are not, so they are not quoted here.
Data honesty

One quarter of these depths are not measurements

Here is the histogram again, but honestly. The single most common depth in the entire global catalogue is exactly 10.0 kilometres — 75,936 events, 26.8 per cent of the file. The second most common is exactly 33.0 kilometres, at 42,506 events.

Neither number is a measurement. They are defaults. Depth is the hardest hypocentral parameter to resolve from distant stations, and when the data cannot constrain it, the analysis pins it to a fixed value and moves on. For decades that value was 33 km — a standard crustal thickness. Modern processing pins it to 10 km instead.

You can watch the convention change. In the decade from 1976, thirty-four per cent of events were filed at exactly 33 km. By 2016 that had fallen to essentially zero, while the share pinned at 10 km climbed from eleven per cent to forty-eight.

Nearly half of all earthquakes recorded this decade have a depth of “10 km,” which means: we do not know.

This does not invalidate the depth histogram — the broad structure, the 300 km minimum, the 700 km cutoff, all survive, because those features live at depths nobody uses as a default. But it does mean the shallow peak is far sharper in the file than it is in the ground.

The rate question

Are there more earthquakes than there used to be?

The count of M4.5+ earthquakes has risen from about 3,450 a year in the late 1970s to about 7,860 a year in the 2020s. That is a 2.3-fold increase, and the trend is one of the most statistically overwhelming things in the dataset: t = 13.2, p ≈ 10−39.

It is also mostly an illusion. Run the same test on large earthquakes — the ones no network could possibly miss, in 1976 or now — and the doubling collapses to a drift. At M5.5, M6.0, M6.5 and M7.0 the fitted trends sit between +17 and +30 per cent over fifty years, with t-statistics between 1.85 and 2.52. Test seven thresholds and a Bonferroni-corrected threshold is p = 0.007; not one of them reaches it.

What grew was the network. Between 1976 and today the number of digital seismic stations reporting to global data centres rose by more than an order of magnitude, and the software that associates their arrivals got very much better. A magnitude 4.6 in the middle of the South Pacific that would have gone unrecorded in 1978 is routine now.

The one place where it is genuinely hard to tell

At the very top of the scale the answer is less clean, and it is worth being precise rather than reassuring. Events of M7.5 and above ran at 3.44 per year in 1976–2000 and 5.28 per year in 2001–2025 — a 53 per cent rise. Annual counts at that size are Poisson (variance/mean = 1.03), and the rise survives deleting the great earthquake cluster of 2004–2012.

But the magnitude scale changed underneath it. In 1976–1985, sixty of the 112 recorded M7+ events carried a surface-wave magnitude, a scale that saturates and systematically under-reports the largest earthquakes. By 2016 essentially every one carries a W-phase moment magnitude, which does not saturate. Across the two halves of the record the mean magnitude of M7+ events rose by 0.09 units. Under a b-value of 1.0, a uniform offset of that size inflates the count above any threshold by 23 per cent on its own.

Correcting for that offset, the residual change is −7 per cent at M7.0 (p = 0.34), +25 per cent at M7.5 (p = 0.09) and +69 per cent at M8.0 (p = 0.09, on thirteen events against twenty-seven). None of these clears a conventional significance threshold, and the correction itself is estimated from the same data it corrects — which is not ideal.

The honest verdict. The doubling of small earthquakes is definitely an artefact. The stability of M7+ is solid. At M7.5 and above, this catalogue cannot settle the question, and neither has the literature: the apparent burst of great earthquakes in 2004–2011 has been tested repeatedly and found consistent with a random Poisson process. “We cannot tell” is the result, not a failure to get one.
Aftershocks

The oldest quantitative law in seismology

In 1894, Fusakichi Omori noticed that aftershocks do not simply fade — they fade at a specific rate. The number per day falls off as one over the time elapsed. Not exponentially, which would give the sequence a characteristic lifetime; as a power law, which gives it none.

On 6 July 2019 a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck near Ridgecrest, California, into one of the densest seismic networks on Earth. In the following year the network catalogued 32,773 aftershocks of magnitude 1.0 or greater within the rupture zone. That is enough to test Omori's observation over five orders of magnitude in time.

Two sequences, different continents, different faults, different instruments, 130 years after Omori: the same exponent to two decimal places.

The largest Ridgecrest aftershock was M5.51 — 1.59 magnitude units below the mainshock. Båth's law, another empirical regularity with no accepted derivation, says that gap should average about 1.2 regardless of mainshock size.

The first five minutes are blind

There is a catch, and it is a good one. Bin the raw Ridgecrest data finely enough and the aftershock rate appears to rise for the first few minutes before it starts falling. Earthquake rates cannot rise after a mainshock and then fall back through the same values; something is wrong.

What is wrong is the seismograms. For minutes after a M7.1, the ground is still ringing from the mainshock and its largest aftershocks, and small events are buried in that coda. They happen; they cannot be picked. The detection floor immediately after the mainshock sits near magnitude 4.2 and takes three days to sink back to its normal 1.2.

Triggering

Two out of every three

Ridgecrest is one sequence. The question it raises is how much of the whole catalogue is sequences — how many of the earthquakes in the file are not independent events at all, but the echoes of earlier ones.

The standard way to ask is declustering: draw a window in space and time around every earthquake, sized by its magnitude, and treat anything that falls inside a larger event's window as triggered. Running the classic Gardner–Knopoff windows over all 283,119 global earthquakes leaves

95,305 independent earthquakes and 187,814 aftershocks.

Two thirds of the catalogue is echo. Apply the windows only forward in time — a stricter convention that refuses to count foreshocks as part of a cluster — and the triggered share falls to 55.6 per cent. Either way, the majority of the earthquakes ever recorded happened because another earthquake happened first.

A caveat worth stating. The Gardner–Knopoff windows were calibrated on southern California in 1974 and are being applied here to the whole planet, including subduction zones they were never fitted to. The 56–66 per cent range is the honest width of the answer, not a precision figure.

Being an aftershock is mostly something small earthquakes do. The share of events that are triggered falls monotonically with size, and it falls a long way:

70%of M4.5–5.0 are triggered
52%of M5.5–6.0
31%of M6.5–7.0
7%of M7.5–8.0

Great earthquakes are overwhelmingly their own cause. That is the same fact the overdispersion measurements showed earlier from a different angle: small-earthquake counts arrive in bursts, great-earthquake counts arrive at random. Here it is stated directly — the burstiness is aftershocks, and aftershocks are small.

Båth's law, and how a detection floor invents a trend

The gap between a mainshock and its largest aftershock is supposed to average about 1.2 magnitude units, independently of how big the mainshock was. Measure it across all 29,980 sequences and it looks like nothing of the sort: the gap climbs steadily from 0.35 at magnitude 5 to 1.57 above magnitude 8. Båth's law appears to be false.

It is not false. It is being truncated. The catalogue stops at magnitude 4.5, so the largest aftershock of a magnitude 5.2 mainshock can be at most 0.7 units below it — any bigger gap is not in the file to be measured. Averaging a quantity whose upper tail has been cut off drags the average down, and it drags it down hardest where the cut is tightest. The result is a rising line that looks like physics and is arithmetic.

Energy

Ten earthquakes, half a century

Magnitude is logarithmic, which everyone knows, and it is easy to underestimate what that does to the accounting. Converting every event to seismic moment and adding them up gives 4.09 × 1023 newton-metres released between 1976 and 2026.

The 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake accounts for 13.8 per cent of it. So does Tohoku in 2011. Ten earthquakes — ten, out of 283,119 — account for 46.4 per cent of all the seismic energy the planet released in half a century. The hundred largest account for 70.4 per cent, leaving the other 283,019 events to share the remaining thirty.

Induced seismicity

Oklahoma turned its earthquakes on, then off

Between 1976 and 2008, the state of Oklahoma and its immediate surroundings produced exactly one earthquake of magnitude 4.5 or greater. In the eleven years from 2009 it produced thirteen.

The cause is not disputed. Oil production in the region brings up enormous volumes of salt water, which is disposed of by injecting it into a deep formation. That raises pore pressure on faults that were already close to failure, and they fail. Counts of M2.5+ events went from 33 in 2009 to 2,927 in 2015.

Then something unusual in earth science happened: the experiment was reversed. Oklahoma's regulator began restricting disposal volumes across the affected area from 2015, tightened the limits regionally in early 2016, and ordered shut-ins around Pawnee after a magnitude 5.8 there in September 2016 — still the largest earthquake in the state's recorded history. What the catalogue shows is the consequence: counts peak in 2015 and fall by an order of magnitude within four years.

The regulatory timeline is context from the public record rather than something this dataset can establish. What the data establishes is the shape of the curve, and that nothing resembling it appears in the preceding thirty-three years.

Explosions

The catalogue remembers every bomb

470 of the records in this file are not earthquakes. They are nuclear explosions, logged by the same instruments, in the same archive, with magnitudes computed the same way.

Sorting them by location reconstructs the geography of the nuclear age without reference to a single treaty document: 152 at Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan, 135 at the Nevada Test Site, 75 at Mururoa and Fangataufa in French Polynesia, 19 at Lop Nur in China, 18 at Novaya Zemlya in the Arctic. A scatter of others across Siberia are the Soviet Union's “peaceful nuclear explosions” — devices used for seismic sounding and to stimulate gas fields.

Sorting them by year reconstructs the arms-control timeline. The annual count runs in the twenties and thirties through the 1980s, collapses after 1990, and stops almost entirely after 1996, the year the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty opened for signature. India and Pakistan appear in 1998. After that there is one signature and only one.

A network built to study earthquakes turns out to be an arms-control instrument that no state can switch off.

That dual purpose is not incidental. Test-ban verification funded a substantial share of twentieth-century seismology, and the global station coverage that makes the rest of this essay possible exists in part because governments wanted to know when other governments set off bombs.

Folklore

Earthquake weather is real, in the instruments

There is a persistent belief that earthquakes prefer certain conditions — a time of day, a kind of weather. It is testable. Bin fifty years of global earthquakes by hour and compare against uniform.

They are not uniform. At M4.5 and above the chi-square statistic is 244 on 23 degrees of freedom, against a 5 per cent critical value of 35.2. The busiest hour runs 6.4 per cent above uniform and the quietest 3.5 per cent below. On its face, earthquakes have a preferred time of day.

Now raise the threshold. At M5.5 the statistic falls to 25.2 and the effect is gone. At M6.0, 19.0. At M7.0, 26.3 — on 707 events, comfortably inside what chance produces.

The mechanism is cultural noise. Traffic, industry and machinery raise the ground-motion noise floor near seismic stations during working hours, and a station that cannot hear a small event cannot contribute to locating it. The pattern is in the listening, not in the shaking.

A trap I walked into first. Running the same test on the dense Southern California catalogue gave an enormous chi-square — 416 at M3.0. It was spurious. A quarter of that catalogue consists of Ridgecrest aftershocks, and the violently clustered first days of the sequence land in a handful of hour bins. Removing the sequence cut the statistic to 68. Any test that assumes independent events must decluster first, and I did not, until the number looked too good.

And the moon, which is the oldest version of the claim

The moon raises a tide in the solid Earth of about thirty centimetres twice a day, and at new and full moon the solar and lunar tides add. The stress this puts on a fault is tiny — a few kilopascals against the megapascals a fault carries — but it is not zero, and the idea that it sets earthquakes off is very old.

Binning fifty years of earthquakes by lunar phase gives a chi-square of 123 against a critical value of 35.2. That looks like a discovery. It is the Ridgecrest trap again, at planetary scale: the catalogue is two-thirds aftershocks, aftershocks arrive in dense bursts, and bursts land unevenly across phase bins. Run the identical test on the 95,305 declustered independent events and the chi-square drops to 20.3 — below the critical value, no signal at all.

There is one residue. Restricting to shallow independent events — the population where the physics predicts tidal triggering should be easiest to see — leaves a 1.2 per cent excess during spring tides, at z = 2.07, p = 0.04. That is in the direction theory expects, and it is consistent with the published result that tidal triggering is real and very small. It is also one test among several run on the same data, and it does not survive correcting for that. Call it suggestive.

What it is emphatically not is the effect folklore describes. A one per cent modulation is not something anyone notices from their kitchen window. If the moon moved earthquakes the way the stories say, this test would have found it in the first thousand events instead of failing to find it in two hundred and eighty thousand.

Method & sources

All earthquake data from the USGS Earthquake Catalog (ComCat), queried through the FDSN event web service between 4 and 5 September 2026. The global set is every M4.5+ event from 1976-01-01 to 2026-09-04, retrieved in annual chunks (283,681 records). Regional sets: Southern California M1.0+ 2015–2026 (146,592 records), Oklahoma and southern Kansas M2.5+ 2009–2019, the Ridgecrest and Kahramanmaraş sequences, and a 30-day global sample at M0.5+. Total 457,408 events.

Plate boundaries after Bird, P. (2003), “An updated digital model of plate boundaries,” Geochemistry Geophysics Geosystems 4(3). On the epicentre map the boundaries are drawn for reference only. In the tectonic-setting analysis Bird's 5,824 boundary steps and their seven-class STEPCLASS codes do the work: every earthquake is assigned to its nearest step by great-circle distance, and only events within 200 km of one are counted.

The local b-value map fits Aki's estimator to every M5.0+ event within 300 km of each node of a 2° grid, and reports nothing where fewer than 120 such events exist. Per-node standard error is about ±0.10, so the map is readable as a pattern and not as a set of individual measurements.

Declustering uses the Gardner & Knopoff (1974) space–time windows, L = 100.1238M+0.983 km and T = 100.5409M−0.547 days below M6.5, 100.0320M+2.7389 days above, with events claimed by the largest available mainshock first. The headline 66.3 per cent applies the windows both forward and backward in time, as Gardner & Knopoff did; the forward-only figure is 55.6 per cent. Aftershock productivity follows Utsu (1970); the mainshock–largest-aftershock gap is Båth (1965). Lunar phase is the elapsed fraction of a 29.530589-day synodic month measured from the new moon of 6 January 2000, which is accurate to well under a bin width over this period.

b-values by the Aki (1965) maximum-likelihood estimator with the Utsu binning correction and Shi & Bolt (1982) uncertainties. Aftershock decay fitted as the Omori–Utsu law by least squares in log-log space. Seismic moment from log M₀ = 1.5 M + 9.1. Trend tests are ordinary least squares on annual counts with a Poisson likelihood-ratio cross-check; reported p-values are uncorrected for multiple comparison, and with seven thresholds tested a Bonferroni threshold would be 0.007.

The epicentre map carries all 283,119 events in the page itself, stored at 0.01° and 0.05-magnitude precision to keep the file to a few megabytes. That rounding moves a handful of events across a magnitude threshold — the map counts 84,871 at M5.0 where the full-precision catalogue has 84,833. Every statistic quoted in the text is computed from the unrounded data.

Analysis and figures built from the raw catalogue; every number on this page is computed from the downloaded files rather than quoted from a secondary source. Where the data could not answer a question — the great-earthquake rate — that is stated rather than smoothed over.
